headline_en: How students going abroad can get certificates attested online
summary_en: A step-by-step explainer on the government's online attestation of educational certificates for people going abroad, run through the MyGov platform (www.mygov.bd) since 1 October 2024. It covers the documents and file formats needed, account registration and profile verification, finding the right application, fees and payment, uploading, tracking and downloading the attested document.

facts.statement: Bangladesh started an electronic (online) system for attesting educational certificates and academic transcripts for people applying to or going to study abroad on 1 October (2024); applicants no longer have to go to the Ministry of Education for attestation of these documents.
For attestation of education-related documents on MyGov, the applicant needs only a National ID (NID) or an online-registered birth registration certificate.

Because the whole MyGov attestation process is online, soft copies of the documents must be scanned in advance; scanned files must be saved in JPEG, JPG or PNG format and each file must be within 1 MB.
The online attestation of certificates for people going abroad is done on the MyGov platform, www.mygov.bd.
Step 1 on MyGov (www.mygov.bd): open an account by giving a name and a mobile number or email address, then set a password; this completes initial registration.

Step 2 on MyGov: after the account is opened a personal profile is created, which must be verified immediately with the NID or birth registration number or year of birth. One NID can verify only one MyGov account.

On the MyGov homepage the first listed service is 'বিদেশগামী নাগরিকদের সার্টিফিকেট সত্যায়ন' (certificate attestation for citizens going abroad); clicking it opens a page with separate application options for attesting each kind of document relevant to going abroad, from which students pick the attestations their foreign institution has asked for. A specific document can also be found through the homepage search box, including by voice command; the wanted application appears at the top of the results.

Each MyGov attestation application option lists what documents are needed, upload rules, the application fee, how to fill in the online form and the processing time; these differ by document type, and processing time is not the same for all documents.
On MyGov some attestation services are free and some carry a set application fee (amounts not given in the article); fees can be paid by online banking, card and mobile payment gateways.
In the MyGov application form, fields marked with a red star are mandatory and the others may be left blank; where applicable a plus (+) button allows adding multiple pages or files.

A MyGov application need not be completed in one sitting: it can be saved as a draft and resumed later by logging in with the mobile number or email and password and going to the 'সেবা ব্যবস্থাপনা' (service management) option.

The applicant cannot move to the next step on MyGov until attachments are fully uploaded. Instead of uploading at each application, all documents can be uploaded to the account right after account verification; relevant ones are then attached automatically when separate applications are submitted.

After final submission each MyGov application gets a unique tracking number; with it the latest status can be seen under 'সেবা ব্যবস্থাপনা' (service management) and on the applicant's personal dashboard.
After the specified number of working days, the successfully attested document appears on the applicant's MyGov dashboard and can be downloaded immediately.
The article advises verifying the MyGov profile first so the whole attestation process runs without interruption, and notes that one NID can verify only one account.

headline_en: The many sorrows of the expatriate
summary_en: A reader's essay from the UAE describing the hardships of Bangladeshi workers abroad: long separation from family, hard labour, financial pressure, isolation, discrimination, and difficulty resettling after return. It gives no figures and calls on the government to pay attention to migrants' mental health and financial security.

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi expatriate writer in the UAE says most Bangladeshi workers in Middle Eastern countries get to go home no more than once a year, and many cannot return for ten to twelve years at a stretch.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says most Bangladeshi migrant workers are in hard manual work abroad such as construction, transport, services or agriculture, working from morning to evening in extreme heat or cold and sending money home at the end of the month.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says that after paying for house building, children's education, bank loan repayment and other family costs, many expatriates cannot keep any savings for themselves and are themselves under financial pressure.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says isolation and lack of direct contact with family leave many expatriates depressed, and that they sometimes need mental health care and counselling which they cannot easily get.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says workplace discrimination, racist behaviour, legal complications and visa problems are common for expatriates, that language or citizenship problems stop them securing their rights, and that in the Middle East in particular many expatriates are denied fair pay even after hard labour.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says returning expatriates need a lot of money to rebuild life in Bangladesh, often cannot reintegrate into work, lose their earnings when they fail to invest them properly, and often get no government support when repaying bank loans or trying to start a business.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The writer calls for special attention to expatriates' mental health and financial security so they can build a proper life after returning, and for a more responsible role from the state and government.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

headline_en: How remittance fighters can be given VIP status
summary_en: An opinion column arguing that Bangladesh neglects remittance senders and proposing a tiered 'Wage Earners Elite Club' card with airport, travel, insurance and social-security benefits, plus a government remittance app. It cites export and remittance figures and the 6 percent incentive on formal-channel remittances. All measures are the writer's proposals, not decisions.

facts.statement: The columnist says Bangladesh's exports in the last fiscal year were about USD 47 billion; assuming about 50 percent value addition, net foreign-currency earnings from exports were about USD 23 billion.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The columnist estimates that, judging by the current trend, remittances this year could be between USD 27 and 30 billion.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The column says remittances sent through official channels receive only a 6 percent incentive, which the writer calls inadequate.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The column says that to remit formally expatriates must go to banks and licensed remittance houses, and describes an unskilled worker in Dubai who, rather than go through an exchange house's complicated and bureaucratic process, phones a hundi operator, agrees an exchange rate and gets money to his family, bypassing formal channels entirely.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The columnist says remittance senders are often treated badly and are not given due respect at airports or at foreign embassies.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The column says the Chief Adviser recently said remittance fighters should be treated as VIPs.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): a government 'Wage Earners Elite Club' listing expatriates in Platinum, Gold, Silver and Bronze tiers according to remittances sent in the previous year, each tier with separate benefits.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): separate immigration and check-in counters for Elite Club members, government-paid airport transport on arrival and departure (private car or bus pick-up and drop by category), and dedicated airport lounge access for Platinum, Gold and Silver cardholders.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): Platinum and Gold cardholders treated as Commercially Important Persons (CIP), honoured with crests at national events and invited to government events; and free round-trip tickets to Bangladesh (business or economy class by category) depending on remittance amount.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): a remittance app for expatriates linked to banks and remittance houses at home and abroad (sending via bank account, mobile wallet or remittance house), showing real-time exchange rates and all fees before the transaction, with biometric login, two-factor security, AML and KYC compliance, real-time tracking by push notification, SMS and email, multiple languages and 24/7 live-chat support.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): promote the app through embassy roadshows and seminars, print, electronic and social media, testimonials and emails via employers and embassies; and use the app's Net Promoter Score and in-app surveys to rate immigration-related services (e.g. visa tracking, residency permit renewal), airport meet-and-greet services and the conduct and performance of embassy staff.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Long-term proposals (not decisions): annual renewal and re-grading of Elite Club cards on the previous year's remittance amount and consistency, with extra benefits such as free return tickets for top performers; life insurance and health care for cardholders' families up to a limit and school priority for their children; customer-service training for embassy and airport staff; and a social safety net of pension schemes, education scholarships for children and government housing loans.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Chairman of Unilever Consumer Care; author of the column proposing a Wage Earners Elite Club and remittance app.

headline_en: 'When remittance fighters come to the airport, they must be addressed as sir'
summary_en: Actor Farhan Ahmed Jovan posted on Facebook on 1 September 2024 that expatriate workers should be addressed as 'sir' and given a secretary's level of respect at the airport. He told Prothom Alo that migrant workers, especially those travelling to and from the Middle East, face the most needless harassment from airport officials.

facts.statement: Actor Farhan Ahmed Jovan wrote on Facebook on Sunday 1 September 2024 that expatriate remittance fighters should be addressed as 'sir' when they come to the airport and be given the same respect a secretary gets at the airport.

Jovan told Prothom Alo that while travelling for shoots he has seen migrant workers suffer the most needless harassment at the airport, with officials much stricter towards them, and that those travelling to and from Middle Eastern countries face it most; he said sincere behaviour matters more than literally saying 'sir'.
facts.source_in_article: Farhan Ahmed Jovan to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The article says stories are heard of passengers waiting hours for luggage at the airport, and that Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus has already spoken, in a statement, giving direction on service to expatriates at the airport.

A commenter named Tahmina Tasnim wrote under Jovan's post that care must be taken that the goods expatriates bring with such hardship are not stolen or damaged at the airport, and that the authorities must take responsibility if they are.

headline_en: Higher education in Ireland: application method, costs, scholarships and facilities
summary_en: A guide for Bangladeshi students to studying in Ireland: entry requirements, universities, admission cycle and documents, the long-stay Type D study visa (submitted via the Irish embassy in New Delhi), fees, processing time, tuition and living costs, scholarships, part-time work rules and post-study work permits.

facts.statement: For undergraduate programmes in Ireland, generally at least 75 percent marks in the higher secondary certificate examination are needed; for postgraduate study the usual condition is a bachelor's degree in the same subject with at least 60 percent. Master's and PhD programmes need a bachelor's in the same or a relevant subject; PhD applicants must show publications and MBA applicants professional experience.
Irish universities check English proficiency through test scores such as IELTS, TOEFL or PTE.

QS world rankings cited by the article: Trinity College Dublin 81, University College Dublin 171, University of Galway 289, University College Cork 292, University of Limerick 426, Dublin City University 436.

Institutions the article lists as top choices in Ireland for international students: American College Dublin, University College Dublin, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin City University, University of Limerick, University College Cork, Maynooth University, Queen's University Belfast, National University of Ireland Galway / University of Galway. Courses named as most important: business analytics, investment banking and finance, data science, medicine science, business management and administration, computer science and IT, medicine and health science, hospitality and tourism management.

Undergraduate admission at Irish universities generally starts in September, with some universities also taking a January intake; postgraduate admission starts at the end of August or in September and ends in May. Applications are made by opening an account on each university's own website and uploading scanned documents; status is shown in the account.

University application checklist for Ireland: completed application form, all previous academic documents and marksheets, passport-size photo, copies of passport and national ID, IELTS certificate, application fee receipt, letter of recommendation; for postgraduate also publications, a personal essay or writing sample and reference letters. Programmes may ask for more.
Application fees at Irish universities vary, generally EUR 45 to 90. After checking documents the university sends an offer letter, which is later used for the visa.

Bangladeshi students going to study in Ireland apply for the long-stay Type D visa, which allows a stay of more than 90 days. The application is made online; the portal keeps the applicant's information for 30 days during the process; the completed form is printed, signed and submitted with documents to the embassy.

Irish student visa documents listed: 2 passport-size photos; passport valid at least 12 months after the date of arrival in Ireland; previous passports if any; statement of purpose; offer letter from the Irish institution; proof of tuition fee payment (EUR 6,000 is the minimum to be shown at immigration, though some institutions may require the full fee); previous academic certificates; English proficiency certificate; proof of work experience where applicable; a personal bank statement of at least EUR 10,000; signed letter and national ID copy of any sponsor; completed financial summary form; private medical insurance of at least EUR 25,000 each for accident and illness; police clearance certificate.
The Irish study-visa financial summary form is at https://www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/IRL-study-visa-financial-summary.docx.
All documents for the Irish student visa must be originals, and any document in Bangla must be supplied with a full English translation.

To submit the Irish visa application, the applicant first takes an appointment at the visa application centre and receives a confirmation email with the date; on that date they attend in person to give biometrics (fingerprints, photo). The embassy address printed is C-17, Malcha Marg, Chanakyapuri, New Delhi, Delhi-110021, India.
For an Irish visa the visa facilitation service charge is INR 3,518 per applicant; the visa fee is INR 5,300 for single entry and INR 9,000 for multiple entry.

An Irish study visa takes 30 working days to 2 calendar months, sometimes longer; the article advises applying 6 to 8 weeks before the travel date. Once decided, the visa and original documents are returned by courier.

Study costs in Ireland as given: public universities EUR 14,000 to 21,000; private institutions EUR 12,000 to 14,000; Institutes of Technology (IoT) EUR 10,000 to 12,500. The article also gives annual costs of EUR 9,850 to 25,500 for bachelor's and EUR 9,500 to 34,500 for master's and doctoral degrees. Medicine and health science is the most expensive subject.

Monthly living costs in Ireland as given: EUR 550 to 1,000 on average in most cities; EUR 1,500 to 1,800 in big cities such as Dublin; EUR 860 to 1,400 in Cork; EUR 800 to 1,100 in smaller cities such as Galway.

Scholarships listed for Ireland: Irish Government International Education Scholarship (up to EUR 10,000 per level, bachelor's, master's or PhD); Higher Education Authority international scholarship (tuition plus EUR 10,000 stipend); Erasmus Mundus (full tuition and monthly allowance for master's); Go Overseas full tuition scholarship; Enterprise Ireland's Education Ireland scholarship (EUR 3,000 to 5,000).

University scholarships listed: UCD Global Excellence Scholarship up to EUR 10,000; University of Limerick International Education Scholarship EUR 3,000; Dublin City University International Scholarship EUR 2,000 to 7,000; National University of Ireland Galway International Student Scholarship up to EUR 5,000; Maynooth University International Master's Scholarship EUR 2,000; Dublin Institute of Technology Centenary Scholarship Programme EUR 10,000.

The article says students in Ireland holding immigration Stamp 2 are covered by a permission to work that stays valid as long as Stamp 2 is valid; they need a Personal Public Service (PPS) number, which the article says is obtained through being hired for a job. Work is allowed 20 hours a week, and full time during winter and summer holidays.
The article says the minimum pay for part-time jobs in Ireland is EUR 733 a month, or about BDT 93,190.

After graduating, a work permit is needed for full-time work in Ireland; fresh graduates mainly use the General Employment Permit or the Critical Skills Employment Permit. Both initially allow up to two years of work, take 28 days to process and allow 40 hours of work a week. The General permit can be renewed for a further three years and not after that; the Critical Skills permit can be renewed every two years. Either can be applied for at least 12 weeks (3 months) before the first day of work.
The article notes that higher education costs in Ireland are somewhat higher than in other EU member states, and that English is the only language needed for study, scholarships and jobs.

headline_en: Expatriates want VIP status for remittance fighters
summary_en: At a reception and Eid reunion in Salmiya, Kuwait on 21 June 2024, the Kuwait branch of Bangladesh Probashi Odhikar Parishad demanded an end to harassment of expatriates at Bangladesh's airports and VIP status for them. They also protested the budget's duty on mobile phones and demanded pensions, health insurance, free repatriation of bodies and interest-free loans.

facts.statement: On Friday 21 June 2024, at a reception and Eid reunion at a restaurant in Salmiya organised by the newly formed committee of Bangladesh Probashi Odhikar Parishad's Kuwait branch, Bangladeshi expatriates in Kuwait demanded that the Bangladesh government stop harassment of expatriates at airports and give them VIP status.

facts.statement: The Kuwait expatriates demanded special budget allocations for a pension for returnee expatriates, health insurance, carrying expatriates' bodies home free of cost, and interest-free loans on easy terms.

headline_en: No proposal has come to take Khaleda Zia abroad: Law Minister
'I learned yesterday how hard it is for a father to carry his son's body'
summary_en: Tanvir Mia alias Sohel (22) of Debgram, Akhaura, Brahmanbaria, whose Malaysia flight arranged through a broker was cancelled on Friday 31 May 2024, fell from a train door into the Meghna river at Bhairab on the way home and died; his body was recovered about 44 hours later. The family had paid BDT 6.5 lakh a year earlier to broker Alamgir Hossain of Noyadil village and his Malaysia-based brother, who have since fled their home.

facts.statement: Tanvir Mia alias Sohel (22) of Debgram village, Akhaura upazila, Brahmanbaria, was returning home with his father on the Upakul Express intercity train on Friday afternoon 31 May 2024 after his Malaysia flight was cancelled when he fell from the train door into the Meghna river while crossing the Bhairab rail bridge in Kishoreganj; his body was recovered about 44 hours later on Sunday 2 June 2024 around midday and buried that evening.

Tanvir's family paid BDT 6.5 lakh (sare chhoy lakh taka) one year before June 2024 to send him to Malaysia through broker Alamgir Hossain of Noyadil village, Akhaura, and Alamgir's Malaysia-based brother.

Broker Alamgir Hossain first gave Tanvir a flight date of 19 January 2024, which was cancelled; a second flight was to be on the morning or midday of Friday 31 May 2024 and its cancellation was announced after the family had travelled to Dhaka. A sub-headline quotes the family that the brokers gave dates two or three times and did not keep their word.
The family trusted the broker because three days earlier he had taken 30 people (to Malaysia); many others were due to go with Tanvir on the cancelled 31 May 2024 flight.
Tanvir's father Meraj Mia sold 130 decimals (shotok) of land to send his son abroad and for his own business.
Father Meraj Mia said the people through whom he tried to send his son to Malaysia made no enquiry after the death and have fled their home; he does not know where they are.

headline_en: Crowds at the airport to go to Malaysia
summary_en: A photo caption from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on 31 May 2024, the deadline for approved Bangladeshi workers to enter Malaysia. It recaps that Malaysia's market reopened in 2022 after four years, a syndicate formed again, and in March 2024 Malaysia said it would take no more workers for now; many could not get air tickets.

facts.statement: Malaysia's labour market reopened for Bangladeshis in 2022 after being closed for four years over irregularities in sending workers through a syndicate; a syndicate was formed again afterwards.
In March 2024 Malaysia said it would not take any more workers for the time being.
Workers who had already received approval and visas had to enter Malaysia by 31 May 2024 (a Friday).

For several days before 31 May 2024, on recruiting agencies' assurances, people from around Bangladesh came to Dhaka to go to Malaysia and crowded Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport every day; many could not get air tickets and were left in uncertainty.

headline_en: Critical patient takes three days just to get from Sandwip to Chattogram
summary_en: Cyclone Remal stopped Sandwip-Chattogram sea crossings for three days from Saturday 25 May 2024, stranding a critically injured boy, a pregnant woman and passengers bound abroad whose visas or tickets were about to expire. On Tuesday 28 May a single speedboat was run by special arrangement for critical patients and foreign-bound passengers.

facts.statement: When Cyclone Remal shut Sandwip-Chattogram sea transport from Saturday (25 May 2024), passengers bound abroad whose visas or tickets were about to expire were stuck on Sandwip island for about three days.

On Tuesday 28 May 2024, at the request of the Sandwip Upazila Nirbahi Officer, one speedboat carried only critical patients and foreign-bound passengers across from Gachhua Amir Mohammad Ghat by special arrangement; Md. Akbar Hossain of Santoshpur union said his flight was that Tuesday evening and he had no option but to cross.

Sandwip UNO Rigyan Chakma said boat movement must stay closed while cautionary signal no. 3 is in force regardless of the actual sea state, while crossings continue when there is no signal even if the sea is very rough; the 28 May 2024 speedboat was requested as a special case for people in distress.

headline_en: Recommendation to give expatriates a special smart card to raise remittances through legal channels
summary_en: On 24 April 2024 the parliamentary standing committee on the finance ministry recommended non-financial incentives alongside the existing financial incentive to boost remittances through banking channels. It recommended a special smart card for remitters and their families giving priority at government hospitals, service offices and with law enforcement, plus smooth airport immigration and customs clearance.

facts.statement: At its meeting in the Jatiya Sangsad building on Wednesday 24 April 2024, the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Finance recommended (a recommendation, not a decision) giving non-financial incentives in addition to the ongoing financial incentive to speed up remittances through legal banking channels, including a special smart card for remittance senders and their family members.

The committee recommended that expatriates' parents, spouses and children get special priority at government hospitals, government service offices and, for protection, with law enforcement agencies, and advised giving hassle-free immigration and customs clearance at airports.

The committee advised using a smart app to raise remittances and taking the necessary steps to issue national ID cards and birth registration certificates to expatriates so they can send money without obstruction.

The meeting was chaired by committee chairman A H M Mustafa Kamal; members and State Minister for Finance Waseqa Ayesha Khan, M A Mannan, A K Abdul Momen, Ahmed Firoz Kabir, A K M Selim Osman and Runu Reza attended.

headline_en: Higher education in Malaysia: costs and facilities
summary_en: A guide for Bangladeshi students to studying in Malaysia: entry requirements, top public universities, tuition costs, intake periods, university and student-visa documents, the EMGS online visa process (VAL in 14 working days, e-visa in 48 hours), what to do on arrival, living costs, part-time work limits, scholarships and the post-study Employment Pass.

facts.statement: The article says Malaysia has more than 2 lakh (200,000) foreign students so far, that Bangladesh ranks high by number of foreign students there, and that students from more than 140 countries study there each year.

General requirements for foreign students at Malaysian universities: at least 12 years of schooling for a bachelor's; a minimum CGPA of 3.50 out of 5 in SSC/HSC/O-level/A-level for bachelor's programmes; a bachelor's degree with a minimum CGPA of 2.5 out of 4 for master's; IELTS 6.5 (varies by programme and university); some programmes also need GRE or GMAT.

The article says Malaysia's public universities are best for low-cost higher education, topped by Universiti Malaya (UM), Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM), Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM), International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) and Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM); popular subjects are MBA, computer science, data science, medicine and health care, and banking and finance.

Depending on university and programme, a 3.5 to 4 year bachelor's in Malaysia can cost MYR 9,600 to 137,500 and a 1 to 2 year master's MYR 7,500 to 12,700; the article gives 1 ringgit as equal to 23 taka.
Malaysian universities generally take applications in two windows: one opening in June each year with a deadline up to September, and one in November with a deadline up to February.

Basic documents for a Malaysian university application: completed application form, high school certificate (for bachelor's), bachelor's certificate (for master's), passport-size photo, valid passport, motivation letter, English proficiency certificate (IELTS or TOEFL), and proof of application fee payment where applicable; requirements differ by university.

Documents for a Malaysian student visa: one passport-size photo on white background (35/45 mm); the first pages of a passport with 18 months' validity (photo and personal details) and any pages with visa stamps; acceptance/offer letter from the Malaysian university; medical report; copies of all academic records with certificates; a personal bond of MYR 750, refunded at the end of study on condition that the student has not broken Malaysian immigration law; English proficiency certificate (IELTS/TOEFL).

Additional documents for a Malaysian student visa: an approval letter from the Malaysian university; a cover letter issued by the university mentioning the student's application to study there; proof of sufficient funds for tuition and living costs; and a pre-VAL (pre Visa Approval Letter) medical report issued in the student's home country, although the student may instead do the pre-VAL medical screening at a registered clinic after arriving in Malaysia. Applicants to public universities must contact their institution for pre-VAL medical instructions.

Bangladeshi students must apply for a student visa before coming to Malaysia; the application can be started online through EMGS (Education Malaysia Global Services), or made through a representative of the chosen university or an EMGS agent. The article describes EMGS as part of Malaysia's Ministry of Higher Education and a one-stop centre for international students at public and private institutions.
The applicant pays a visa processing fee for the Malaysian student visa, which varies by university and programme (no amount given).

The Visa Approval Letter (VAL) for Malaysia is issued 14 working days after the application is submitted, and status can be checked meanwhile. Bangladeshi students also need an e-visa to enter Malaysia, which the article says can be obtained within 48 hours.

After arriving in Malaysia: within the first seven days do medical screening at any EMGS-registered clinic; in the first month arrange housing, check with the institution and EMGS that academic documents are in order, and collect from the university the Student Pass (a sticker in the passport) and the i-Kad (the foreign student identity card that confirms legal stay in Malaysia).
The article says accommodation, food, transport, medical, phone and internet and bank account in Malaysia together may cost about USD 170 to 180 (the period is not stated in the article).

Foreign students in Malaysia are allowed at most 20 hours of part-time work, counted across semester breaks or weekend holidays, tied to the validity of the Student Pass; applications for part-time work must be made through the student's own institution. The article advises looking for work on campus (library, cafe, office reception).

Scholarships named for Malaysia: Malaysian government scholarship, Malaysia Commonwealth Scholarship and Fellowship Plan, and Malaysian International Scholarship; many universities also have their own scholarships, grants and tuition waivers, and loans, tuition waivers and education funds exist.

After study, a foreign graduate must first secure a job in Malaysia; the employer then handles the work permit, also called the Employment Pass, valid for a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 5 years. The passport should have at least 18 months' validity when applying for the work permit.

headline_en: Accused allegedly snatched from police after attack in Faridpur
summary_en: On Friday 1 March 2024 in Majhardia village, Saltha, Faridpur, Md. Turap Molla (45), a warrant-listed accused in a human trafficking and murder case, escaped after police arrested him; locals say relatives attacked police and snatched him, which police deny. A local leader says he is the main accused over a man taken to Libya on a promise of Italy, tortured and killed.

facts.statement: According to local Swechchhasebak League leader Md. Faruk Hossain, on 12 February 2023 a man named Nur Alam of Majhardia village, Saltha, Faridpur was taken to Libya on the promise of being sent to Italy, tortured and killed (the article's wording attaches the date 12 February 2023 to the incident).
facts.source_in_article: Md. Faruk Hossain, local Swechchhasebak League leader

facts.statement: Md. Turap Molla (45) of Majhardia village, Majhardia union, Saltha, Faridpur, described by a local leader as a manpower broker ('adam byabsayi'), is the main accused in the human trafficking and murder case over Nur Alam's death, and a court has issued an arrest warrant against him.

On Friday 1 March 2024 around Jumma prayers, a Saltha police team led by ASI Nazmul Hossain arrested Turap Molla in front of the Eidgah mosque in Majhardia west para; locals and the UP chairman Md. Afsar Uddin Matubbar say his brothers, nephews and relatives then snatched him from police, while ASI Nazmul Hossain says there was no attack: family members pushed Turap down and he ran away.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Faruk Hossain; UP chairman Md. Afsar Uddin Matubbar; ASI Nazmul Hossain

facts.statement: Faridpur Assistant Superintendent of Police (Nagarkanda Circle) Md. Asaduzzaman said several police teams were in the field to catch Turap Molla and he hoped to arrest him quickly.
The case illustrates the route in which a person from Faridpur is promised Italy but is taken to Libya and tortured there.

headline_en: 63 Bangladeshis in Malaysia surviving on mashed potato and lentils
summary_en: At least 63 young men from Gangni upazila, Meherpur, who went to Malaysia in November 2023 have been confined for three months in a three-storey building in Kuala Lumpur without work, with passports taken and visas mostly expired. Each paid BDT 4 to 5 lakh to three related local brokers working with an unnamed Dhaka travel agency in Banani; the district administration advised families to file cases but none agreed.

facts.statement: At least 63 young men from four villages of Kazipur union and Mohammadpur village of Motmura union, Gangni upazila, Meherpur, who went to Malaysia for labour work in November 2023, said on 11 February 2024 that they had been held for three months on the ground and first floors of a three-storey building in Kuala Lumpur with no work, not allowed outside, and living on two meals a day of mashed potato and lentils.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: On landing in Malaysia, agency people took the workers by vehicle to a building and took away all their passports; they were promised work within one month (elsewhere: within 40 days of arrival) but three months passed without any job.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Suruj Ali and Awal of Sahebnagar village and Abdullah of Mohammadpur village (Gangni, Meherpur), who are cousins, took BDT 4 to 5 lakh from each of the men to take them to Malaysia for labour jobs.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The Meherpur men were promised construction labour jobs in Malaysia at a monthly salary of BDT 45,000 to 50,000 within 40 days of arrival; none received any work.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The victims say 54 of them were taken on 6 November 2023 to an agency's office on Road 4, Banani, Dhaka, stayed there several days, and were flown from Dhaka airport to Malaysia on one flight at about 6 pm on 11 November 2023.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The confined men said almost all of their visas had expired; they live crammed into a few rooms; potatoes, lentils and rice are delivered morning and night by Chinese and Malaysian nationals who do not talk, threaten them when they ask about work and tell them to contact those who sent them from Bangladesh. Many have become mentally and physically ill and said they might be driven to suicide.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Kazipur union ward 1 UP member Faruk Hossain said more than a hundred people from Kazipur and nearby areas went to Malaysia hoping for good work, arranged by a travel agency in Dhaka, and none of them got work.
facts.source_in_article: Faruk Hossain, UP member, Kazipur union ward 1

facts.statement: Abdullah of Mohammadpur village told Prothom Alo by phone that 'some trouble happened in Malaysia' so work could not be given, that everyone would get work within the month (he hoped by 28 February 2024), and that those who do not get work would be brought home after getting visas affixed; he did not answer whether they would get their money back. He said he is a computer operator at the Dhaka travel agency. Main broker Suruj Ali's phone was switched off.
facts.source_in_article: Abdullah, by phone to Prothom Alo; reporter

facts.statement: Sathi Khatun, wife of Rashidul of Kazipur, said her husband went to Malaysia by selling one decimal (shotok) of homestead land and taking a BDT 3 lakh loan at high interest, has had no work, and has no way to return. Shilpi Khatun, wife of Rubel, said her husband cannot eat three meals, cries daily to come home, and the family has nothing left to sell to bring him back.
facts.source_in_article: Sathi Khatun and Shilpi Khatun, wives of stranded workers

facts.statement: Meherpur Deputy Commissioner Md. Shamim Hasan said the matter was discussed at the district law and order committee meeting on Sunday 11 February 2024 and the victims' families were advised to file a case, but none of them agreed to file one.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Shamim Hasan, Deputy Commissioner, Meherpur

facts.statement: The workers sent five video clips pleading to be rescued; Prothom Alo spoke to them by WhatsApp video call on Sunday 11 February 2024.
